extracted.intended_audience: architects, builders, conservators, patrons, and educated readers interested in architectural aesthetics and preservation
extracted.subtask_description: Normative principles for designing domestic and public architecture, choosing styles and materials, ornamentation with meaning, and the ethical preservation (not restoration) of historic buildings. Emphasises longevity, fitness to social/political life, and consideration for posterity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic architecture as moral duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Build dwellings with care, patience, fondness, and diligent completion, with a view to their duration; domestic buildings are moral duties and embodiments of household religion and piety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat small habitations respectfully as well as large ones; invest narrow worldly circumstance with dignity; the house should record to children what the family has been (e.g., leave blank stones for inscriptions). Anti-pattern: indifferent, slovenly, or temporary housing that sacrifices stability and rest for illusory liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale of house relative to builder's condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Houses should be built on a scale commensurate with the builder's condition at the commencement of their career rather than on the attainments at its termination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This encourages houses that can stand as long as human work at its strongest and serve as a truthful record of origin rather than speculative over-extension judged by later means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of individual character in domestic design
rubrics_metrics.description: Dwellings should have differences that suit and express each man's character, occupation, and partly his history; the first builder's right over the house should be respected by descendants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow ornaments, inscriptions, and stylistic choices that reflect the owner's life—examples include carved inscriptions on cottages and personal motifs. Avoid enforced uniformity that erases personal or historical identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical purpose and intelligible ornament in public buildings
rubrics_metrics.description: Public buildings should have a definite historical purpose; ornament and sculptural decoration should express symbolically or literally national feeling, achievement, or civic virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not place any ornament on great civic buildings without some intellectual intention. Use bas-reliefs, groups, or symbols to record events or moral ideas (example: capitals of the ducal palace at Venice devoted to Justice, Judgment of Solomon, virtues and vices). Where costume complicates direct representation, employ bold imaginative treatment and frank symbolism rather than empty decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer narrative/meaningful work over meaningless richness
rubrics_metrics.description: Better the rudest work that tells a story or records a fact than the richest work without meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ornament should be judged by its communicative/intellectual content as much as by its technical richness. Avoid purely fanciful or repetitive ornament that has no historical or symbolic purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and build for posterity (long-range usefulness)
rubrics_metrics.description: When we build, we should think that we build for ever; construct with regard to future generations' benefit rather than only for present use or delight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes practicing present economy or self-denial for successors (planting trees, raising cities for future nations). The farther off the intended aim the richer the fruit of labour; design choices should favour long-term usefulness and moral exemplarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glory of a building lies in its age; design for enduring voicefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest glory of a building is not in its stones or gold but in its Age—its ability to be a lasting witness and to acquire 'voicefulness' through long human association.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange larger masses as the principal compositional concern rather than small perishable details; accept and even plan for the beauty imparted by time and weather-staining so that the building's details will be appropriate centuries hence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picturesqueness (parasitical sublimity) — definition and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Picturesqueness is 'Parasitical Sublimity': a kind of beauty arising when sublimity is found in accidental or external qualities rather than in the essential character of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise when shadow, ruggedness, excrescent attributes (hair, mane, shaggy hide, variegation) are being emphasized parasitically. Picturesque treatment can be valuable but is distinct from pure, essential art; don't substitute accidental effects (ivy on a shaft) for fundamental architectural character. Use the picturesque where consistent with inherent character, and as an exponent of age rather than as mere simulated decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match style to material durability
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose architectural styles according to the durability and decomposition properties of accessible materials: styles dependent on points of shade (picturesque/French Gothic) suit materials that weather; styles dependent on purity of line (Italian Gothic, classical) require hard, undecomposing stones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using brick, sandstone, or soft limestone, adopt styles that gain by partial wearing; if using granite, serpentine, or crystalline marbles, employ styles that rely on clear, pure outlines. The nature of available materials should authoritatively determine stylistic choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation over restoration — do not 'restore' historic buildings
rubrics_metrics.description: Restoration, as commonly practiced, is total destruction and a Lie: it cannot recall the spirit of the original workman and results in conjectural copying and cold imitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid restoration that destroys old fabric; if necessary demolition is required, do it honestly. Prefer continuous, faithful maintenance: timely lead sheets on roofs, clearing water-courses, tying loosened stones with iron, staying with timber—'better a crutch than a lost limb.' Anti-patterns: neglect followed by reconstruction; dashing old work to pieces and replacing with basest imitation; deliberate neglect to create work for masons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral prohibition against destroying others' monuments
rubrics_metrics.description: We have no right to touch or obliterate buildings left by past generations; monuments belong in part to their builders and in part to all future generations and should not be destroyed for present convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Destruction for contemporary advantage (formal squares, planted walks, or quays) is ethically unjustified. Treat monuments as communal inheritance with rights that persist beyond original owners; civic decisions must consider posterity and cultural continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active guardianship and continuous care of monuments
rubrics_metrics.description: Monuments should be actively watched, guarded, and repaired at any cost to prevent decay and the false need for restoration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count stones as jewels; set watches, bind loose parts with iron, prop with timber where necessary, and accept temporary unsightliness of supports. Early, preventive measures (small repairs, clearing drains) will save buildings from irreversible ruin.
